headline: An American Among the Dead Puts Joining Saudi Strikes on a Clock
deck: Saudi civil aviation said 12 died at Riyadh's King Khalid airport, including an American; Trump said Washington may join Saudi strikes.
body: Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA), further to its earlier statement, clarified on 11 October that the Saturday attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh resulted in 12 fatalities, including four Saudi citizens and residents of the following nationalities: two Bangladeshi, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian, and one Sudanese, the Saudi Press Agency reported [E1].
The attack also left 309 others injured, including individuals in critical condition, GACA said [E2].
All injured individuals are receiving the necessary medical care at several hospitals, GACA said [E3].
GACA said the attack also caused property damage, the extent of which is currently being assessed [E4].
Several people were wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Reuters reported Saturday [E5].
A medical source at a local hospital said at least two people had been killed Saturday, Channel NewsAsia reported [E10].
The source identified one as an Egyptian flight attendant for a Saudi airline, and the other as a Palestinian with Egyptian travel documents, Channel NewsAsia reported [E10].
Without mentioning the Houthis by name, the aviation authority said the number of injured from Saturday's attack was still being assessed, Channel NewsAsia reported [E8].
Saturday's first reports and GACA's Sunday clarification disagree on how many were killed and injured [E1][E2][E5][E8][E10].

Reuters reported that Saudi civil-aviation authorities suspended operations [E5]. Airport operations had been temporarily suspended pending assessment of the damage, Channel NewsAsia reported [E8]. The BBC said operations at King Khalid International Airport have been suspended [E12].

Associated Press reported that a missile struck a complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights at the Riyadh airport and many people were wounded, according to a regional official who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media [E11].
Several ambulances were seen rushing there, the Associated Press reported [E11].
CNN said Saturday's strike was the third attack this week on Riyadh's international airport, as Iran-backed Houthis escalated the campaign they launched this summer against the kingdom [E13].
A diplomatic source attributed the attack to a Houthi missile, Channel NewsAsia reported [E7].
The head of the Houthi media office said in a post on X after the attack that the group had "shut down Riyadh international airport," CNN reported [E14].

Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki, spokesman for the coalition forces, said the attack on a passenger terminal at the airport on Saturday constituted a war crime under international humanitarian law, Arab News reported [E15].

"The attack on King Khalid International Airport is a terrorist act and will be met with a firm response," Al-Maliki said in a statement released on X and carried by the Saudi Press Agency, Arab News reported. The statement named Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militia and condemned the attack as an act that violated fundamental principles and values [E16].

Asked on Saturday whether he had changed his mind about joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis, President Donald Trump said: "We may." "We're going to look at it," he told reporters in front of the White House, Channel NewsAsia reported [E9]. Reuters reported that Trump said the United States might join Saudi strikes against Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis [E6].
Channel NewsAsia said US media outlets have reported that previous Saudi requests for American military assistance in dealing with the Houthis have been rebuffed [E9].
Since this paper's 9 October file that Trump would not resume strikes on Iran before 3 November, the new fact is Trump saying Washington may join Saudi strikes.

**The desk's reading.** GACA's revision, with an American among the dead, puts Washington's join-strikes line on an operational clock that Saturday's first take did not. Saturday's first take was Reuters's several wounded, a hospital source's at least two dead, and GACA still assessing injuries without naming the Houthis. Trump answered "We may" and "We're going to look at it" that day. Sunday's statement names 12 dead, including a US citizen, and 309 injured. Attribution of the strike remains disputed: a diplomatic source attributed a Houthi missile, the coalition blamed Yemen's Houthis, GACA did not name them, and the Houthi media office said the group had shut down the airport. The competing reading is that "We're going to look at it" remains a comment, previous Saudi requests for American military assistance having been reported rebuffed, and that a casualty revision does not issue an order.

**The next test.** A published order, or a named Pentagon or White House statement, that US forces will join Saudi strikes, by 12:00 UTC on 12 October. If the only new words by then are another comment, the competing reading holds.

flashpoint.note: GACA put Saturday's dead at 12, including one American. Houthi attribution for the strike remains disputed.
